XXII. A well-established legal theory, proposition, or doctrine that is typically stated in Latin is called
a legal maxim. The majority of these Latin maxims originate from European countries that used
Latin as their official language throughout the middle ages. These guidelines enable courts all over
the world to settle cases before them by applying the law as it stands in a fair and reasonable way.
Although such concepts are not legally binding, they do acquire legal status and provide the basis
for good decisions when courts apply them to decide cases or when the legislature adopts them to
pass laws. www.lawpreptutorial.com
To avoid utilizing lengthy definitions, we refer to it as a single word or phrase. For instance, the
maxim "ab initio," which translates to "from the beginning of" or "from the beginning of anything,"
may be used in place of drafting a statement and is equally helpful in practice. The views of early
English philosophers about the application of legal maxims are praiseworthy. According to Thomas
Hobbes' assertion in "Doctor and Student," legal maxims are just as powerful as laws and actions.
Every act or piece of legislation is drafted with a specific goal in mind. Interpreting the provisions
so as to avoid obstructing the lawmakers' intent is a significant duty of the judiciary. By providing
a framework and criteria for interpreting the law, legal maxims play a crucial role in supporting

XIV. The ongoing Sabarimala reference before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court has revived
a foundational constitutional debate on the relationship between Articles 25 and 26 and the
continued validity of the Essential Religious Practice (ERP) test. The ERP test emerged from
an obiter observation in Durgah Committee v. Syed Hussain Ali (1961), where the Court
stated that only those practices which are “essential and integral” to a religion deserve
protection under Article 26. This modified the earlier approach in Shirur Mutt (1954), where
the Court had principally distinguished between secular practices, which can be regulated,
and religious practices, which receive constitutional protection. The present reference
therefore raises a central issue: whether courts should continue identifying essential religious
practices, or whether the inquiry should only be whether a practice is religious or secular.
During the hearing, Justice BV Nagarathna suggested that once a practice is determined to be
strictly secular, everything else would fall within the religious sphere, making the ERP test
unnecessary. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, however, noted that even such a distinction
would still require the Court to evolve standards for deciding what counts as religious and
what counts as secular, thereby bringing the inquiry back to the same constitutional problem.
Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan argued that the ERP test should be abandoned
because Articles 25 and 26 themselves are clear, and that religious affairs should be
understood through the constitutional text rather than broad judicial labels. In his
submission, Article 25(1), which is expressly made “subject to the other provisions” of Part III,
should be read as subject mainly to horizontal equality provisions such as Articles 15(2), 17,
23, and 24, whereas Article 26 stands on a stronger footing because it does not contain the
same phrase.
A major interpretive issue is whether Article 26(b), which protects a denomination’s right to
manage its own affairs in matters of religion, is subject to Article 25(2)(b), which permits the
State to enact laws for social reform and temple entry for all classes and sections of Hindus.
Article 25(2)(b) permits the State to make laws for social welfare and reform, including
throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of
Hindus. Article 26(b) protects a denomination’s right to manage its own affairs in matters of
religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Sai Deepak argued that Article 26 is not
controlled by Article 25(2), and that denominational rights were deliberately insulated from
broader constitutional limitations. In contrast, Senior Advocate Gopal Subramanium argued
that Article 26 must be harmonised with Article 25(2)(a) and (b), so that denominational
temples may still be subject to reform laws opening access to excluded classes. Thus, the
reference now squarely presents two major constitutional questions: whether the ERP doctrine
should survive, and how individual religious freedom under Article 25 must be reconciled with
collective denominational autonomy under Article 26. [Word Count: 484]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.livelaw.in/top-
stories /sabarimala-reference-supreme-court-debates-essential-religious-practice-test-
denominational-rights-vs-state-reform-power-531226

XVII. India's Employability Crisis: India produces over 3 million graduates annually, yet only about
half are considered employable by industry standards. This creates a paradox: thousands of
educated young people remain unemployed while companies struggle to find skilled workers. The
problem is not a shortage of graduates but a fundamental mismatch between what students learn
and what employers need. Engineering and commerce graduates often end up working as clerks or
machine operators—roles that don't require their qualifications—because they lack practical
experience and industry exposure.
The education system emphasizes rote learning and memorization for exams rather than
developing critical thinking and communication skills. Employers consistently report that only
50% of graduates can handle communication-based roles effectively, and merely 44% demonstrate
adequate creative thinking ability. Young people graduate with theoretical knowledge but cannot
solve real-world problems. Additionally, gender and geography create barriers: male graduates
show 43.4% employability compared to 41.7% for females, and Delhi leads at 53.4% employability
while states like Uttar Pradesh and Assam lag significantly behind.
Government initiatives like Skill India and the National Education Policy 2020 promise
improvements, but implementation remains patchy. Private companies offer training programs,
but these mostly benefit students from top-tier colleges. Until curriculum reforms prioritize skill
development, internship programs expand significantly, and training scales across all regions and
social groups, educated unemployment will persist. The solution requires not just more jobs but
fundamental education system transformation aligned with actual industry needs.
Source: India Today Education, India Skills Report 2026, November 2025

rather than within small family groups.
A family historian disagreed. She argued that a successful dinner does not prove that the seating
pattern itself caused wider interaction. In her view, the conversation may have depended on
personal interests, age, profession, humour, or people speaking across the table rather than only to
those seated beside them.
The family committee decided to review the seating notes and feedback cards before deciding
whether to repeat the same seating principle next year.

passages.LOG-P0155:
XVIII. Microplastics—plastic particles smaller than five millimeters—have become ubiquitous in marine
environments, with concentrations increasing dramatically over the past two decades. These
particles originate from various sources: breakdown of larger plastic debris, synthetic clothing
fibers released during washing, and microbeads from personal care products. Marine organisms
frequently ingest microplastics, mistaking them for food, which can cause physical harm by
blocking digestive tracts and reducing nutrient absorption. More concerning is the chemical
dimension: microplastics absorb persistent organic pollutants from surrounding water, potentially
concentrating toxins that then bioaccumulate up the food chain. Research indicates that fish
consumed by humans contain measurable microplastic levels, raising questions about long-term
human health impacts. While some countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics, addressing
microplastics comprehensively requires tackling larger plastic pollution issues, including improved
waste management systems and reducing single-use plastic production globally.
Source: With edits from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Ocean
Pollution Research
passages.LOG-P0156:
XVI. Urban green spaces—parks, gardens, and tree-lined streets—provide significant mental health
benefits to city residents. Studies across multiple countries demonstrate that people living near
parks report lower stress levels, reduced anxiety, and fewer symptoms of depression compared to
those in areas with minimal vegetation. The mechanism appears multifaceted: green spaces
encourage physical activity, facilitate social interaction, and provide psychological restoration
through natural settings. Notably, even brief exposure to nature, such as a 20-minute walk in a
park, can measurably reduce cortisol levels, a key stress hormone. City planners increasingly
recognize these benefits, with many municipalities now prioritizing green infrastructure in urban
development projects. However, access to quality green spaces remains unequal, with lower-
income neighbourhoods typically having fewer parks and less tree coverage, potentially
exacerbating existing health disparities in urban populations.
Source: Adapted from American Psychological Association public health research summaries

 II. Maya visited the Library at some point before the Museum.

passages.LOG-P0162:
XIX. The shift to remote work during recent years has challenged conventional assumptions about
workplace productivity. Initial concerns that working from home would reduce employee output
have not materialized in most sectors. Studies tracking productivity metrics show that remote
workers often match or exceed the performance of their office-based counterparts, with some
companies reporting productivity gains of 5-10%. Several factors contribute to this outcome:
elimination of commute time allows more rest or work hours, fewer office distractions enable
deeper focus, and flexibility helps employees work during their peak performance hours. However,
these benefits are not universal. Jobs requiring extensive collaboration, creative brainstorming, or
hands-on training have proven more challenging to execute remotely. Additionally, some
employees report feeling isolated and struggle to maintain work-life boundaries when their home
becomes their office. Organizations are increasingly adopting hybrid models that attempt to
capture remote work's benefits while preserving valuable aspects of in-person collaboration.
Source: With edits from Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research

passages.LOG-P0165:
XIV. The Constitution of India did not emerge overnight; it was the outcome of a long constitutional
struggle that began under colonial rule and culminated in a representative Constituent Assembly.
The demand for such an Assembly, made by leaders like M.N. Roy and the Indian National
Congress, was finally accepted by the British through the [Q1] of 1946, which laid down the
framework for electing a body to draft a free India’s Constitution.
Under this plan, the Constituent Assembly of India was created in 1946 with an original strength
of 389 members, drawn from British Indian provinces and princely states through indirect
elections and nominations rather than universal adult franchise. The Assembly held its first
meeting on [Q2], with [Q2] as the temporary chairman, and later elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad as
its permanent president to steer the constitution-making process.
In its early sittings, the Assembly debated the basic philosophy of the future Constitution and, on
[Q3], Jawaharlal Nehru moved the historic [Q3], which was later adopted and became the basis of
the [Q3]. After Partition in 1947, the membership of the Assembly was reduced from 389 to [Q4],
and over nearly three years, in eleven sessions, these members deliberated on fundamental rights,
federalism, and the structure of government. The Constitution was finally adopted on [Q5] and
came into force on [Q5], transforming the Constituent Assembly into the Parliament of
independent India.
passages.LOG-P0166:
XVI. In December 2025, a new conversation about work-life balance started in the Indian Parliament
with the introduction of the "Right to Disconnect Bill." This private member’s bill aims to give
employees the legal right to ignore work-related calls, emails, and messages after their official
working hours end. The goal is to protect workers from the "always-on" culture that has become
common in the digital age, where smartphones turn homes into 24/7 offices. The bill proposes
setting up an Employees’ Welfare Authority to enforce these rules and requires companies with
more than 10 employees to clearly define when a workday starts and ends. However, many
business leaders are worried about how this would work in reality. They argue that in sectors like
IT, consulting, and startups, flexibility is key to competing globally. If Indian companies cannot
respond to international clients immediately because of strict "disconnect" laws, they might lose
business to other countries. There is also a fear that such rigid rules could backfire, leading
employers to micromanage workers during office hours to make up for lost time. While the bill is
unlikely to become a law immediately, it has successfully forced a national debate on mental
health and the blurring lines between our personal and professional lives.
Source: Based on analysis of the Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025 from The Times of India.
passages.LOG-P0167:
XVII. The rise of the gig economy has created significant legal challenges regarding worker
classification. Companies like Uber and DoorDash classify their workers as independent
contractors rather than employees, allowing them to avoid providing benefits such as health
insurance, paid leave, and unemployment protection. This classification benefits companies
financially but leaves workers without traditional employment protections. Supporters argue that
gig work offers flexibility that many workers value, allowing them to set their own schedules and
work for multiple platforms simultaneously. Critics counter that this flexibility comes at too high a
cost, as workers bear all business risks—including vehicle maintenance, fuel costs, and income
volatility—without the safety net that employee status would provide. Several states have
attempted to reclassify gig workers as employees, but companies have successfully lobbied against
such measures, arguing that reclassification would eliminate the flexibility that makes gig work
attractive and potentially reduce earning opportunities. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Source: Extracted and edited from Source: Adapted from Brookings Institution economic policy
research

Captain Alistair Finch. The entries describe his final voyage to the remote "Isle of Whispers,"

standard navigational terms and the Captain's peculiar shorthand. The relevant fragments are

     •   Fragment 1: "Reached the cove at dawn. From the lone palm, proceeded thus: twenty

     •   Fragment 2: "The true path is not written plainly. Heed the symbols on the old

passages.LOG-P0169:
XV. Amid loud protests from the opposition, the Karnataka Legislative Assembly on December 18
passed the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, in Belagavi. The
legislation prescribes imprisonment of one to seven years along with fines for hate crimes. For
repeat offences, imprisonment ranges from two to seven years with higher fines. The Bill covers
communication made in public through verbal, print, public, or electronic means.
While tabling the Bill, Home Minister G. Parameshwara cited a Supreme Court ruling delivered
on May 5 this year, which emphasised the need for firm action against communal hate. He noted
that hate speech had led to killings and inter-community violence, harming social harmony. The
legislation aims to protect constitutional values by addressing discrimination rooted in religion,
race, caste, gender, language, and other identities. According to Parameshwara, the objective is to
curb and prevent dissemination, publication, or promotion of hate speech that causes disharmony
or hatred against a person or group. The home minister explained that existing preventive
restrictions on provocative speech were insufficient. Alerts about potential inflammatory speech
could lead to temporary bans, but this was not a long-term solution. Therefore, a separate law was

required, as provocative speeches were often followed by violent incidents. The government is
authorised to direct the removal of hate speech material from media platforms. Hate crime under
the Bill is defined as communicating or promoting hate speech to cause disharmony, enmity, or ill-
will against individuals or groups.
The Bill makes hate speech a cognizable, non-bailable offence, and offenders can be tried by a
Judicial Magistrate First Class. For organisations, persons in charge at the time of the offence are
deemed liable.
The Congress government-initiated discussions on a hate speech law in June after a series of
communal killings in coastal Karnataka, beginning with the lynching of a Muslim man, Ashraf, in
April. Leader of the opposition R. Ashok opposed the Bill, tearing a copy in the assembly and
claiming it infringed on Article 19(1), which guarantees free expression. He argued that police
could misuse the law for political purposes, targeting journalists and opposition members. Ashok
suggested existing provisions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita were adequate. The debate
intensified after Urban Development Minister Byrathi Suresh made a remark directed at BJP
MLA Vedavyas Kamath, prompting the opposition to demand its removal from the official record.
Despite protests, Parameshwara appealed for support, and the speaker announced the Bill had
been approved through a voice vote before adjourning the House for lunch. BJP MLAs later stated
they were caught off guard by the passage without full debate. Minister for Law H.K. Patil
emphasised that the Bill had been passed and could not be discussed again. The Bill seeks to
address communal disharmony by making hate speech and hate crimes punishable under clear
statutory provisions, ensuring swift action against offenders and promoting social harmony in
Karnataka.
Source: The Wire dated Article 19» December 2025
passages.LOG-P0170:
XVIII. In the northern reaches of the ancient kingdom of Lyr, navigators followed a strict code known
as the "Path of the Four Pillars." Travel between the four sacred cities—Keld, Vorin, Sarn, and Tael—
was governed by both celestial rules and conditional edicts passed down through song. The core
principle was that no direct journey could reverse the sacred order: Keld → Vorin → Sarn → Tael was
considered a forward "Sun Path," and its reverse a forbidden "Shadow Path." Specifically, any journey
from a city to the city immediately preceding it in the sacred order was forbidden at all times. Thus,
Vorin → Keld, Sarn → Vorin, and Tael → Sarn were prohibited. However, exceptions existed for "tide-
turn" days, when the sequence Vorin → Keld was permitted if, and only if, the journey was part of a
longer route ending in Sarn. Furthermore, messengers carrying the White Sigil could never visit Sarn
immediately after Tael, and those carrying the Black Sigil could not begin their route in Vorin. Routes
were always a sequence of distinct cities, and navigators strictly adhered to these rules when planning
their voyages.
passages.LOG-P0171:
XV. Between 1946 and 1949, the Constituent Assembly of India functioned as a forum entrusted with the
task of framing a constitutional framework for a newly independent nation. The Assembly was
composed of representatives drawn from diverse regions, communities, and ideological backgrounds,
many of whom had actively participated in the freedom struggle or in provincial governance under
colonial rule. Its meetings were marked by extensive deliberations, disagreements, and revisions,
reflecting the competing visions of governance, liberty, and social justice that existed at the time.
Several sub-committees were constituted to examine specific issues such as fundamental rights,
minority protections, the structure of the judiciary, and the distribution of powers between the Union
and the provinces. Draft proposals were circulated, debated clause by clause, and frequently
reconsidered in light of objections raised by members. The Assembly’s proceedings often reflected
concerns about maintaining national unity while simultaneously addressing historical inequalities and
safeguarding individual freedoms. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Debates within the Assembly also revealed differing attitudes toward judicial power, legislative
supremacy, and the extent to which constitutional provisions should limit future governments. Some
members expressed apprehension about granting excessive discretion to the judiciary, while others
emphasised the need for enforceable guarantees to prevent the abuse of state power. Comparative
constitutional models from other jurisdictions were occasionally referred to, though the members
repeatedly stressed the importance of adapting such ideas to Indian conditions.
The Assembly ultimately adopted the Constitution after multiple readings and revisions, leaving the
task of interpretation and implementation to future institutions within the constitutional framework.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Oxford Constitutional Law, "The Indian Founding: a
comparative perspective," Oxford Constitutions (OUP, 2028), available
at: https: //oxcon.ouplaw.com/display/10.1093/law /9780198704898.001.0001/law-9780198704898-
chapter-4

SECTION IV
XV. The Supreme Court has remarked that it is high time the Commission for Air Quality
Management (CAQM) realized that inordinate delay in finding solutions to worsening Air Quality
Index (AQI) will lead to further complications. The court issued directions to identify causes as
well as their long-term solutions, highlighting that the statutory expert body was asked to revisit
measures to address issues highlighted in previous orders. The Amicus Curiae has highlighted
issues like vehicular pollution with the suggestion that to curb and minimize it, steps like
transition to electric vehicles, a push for public transport, and improved enforcement like
Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) are essential.
For industrial pollution, solutions like fuel transition and emission standards have been
suggested, alongside compliance with Solid Waste Management Rules. The report also highlighted
issues like road and construction dust, firecrackers, and crop residue burning. The judiciary has
been taking up the matter from time to time, issuing directions based on expert reports. However,
the persistence of the crisis underscores a gap between judicial mandate and executive
enforcement. The need of the hour includes effective mass transport systems to limit the number
of vehicles, stringent and corruption-free pollution control norms, and re-arranging timings of
offices and educational institutions. These are not merely administrative adjustments but
essential components of environmental rule of law necessary to contain degradation.
Source: Excerpted and adapted from Down To Earth and Supreme Court proceedings coverage
(January 2026).
passages.LOG-P0175:
XV. ‘Transferable property refers to property that can be legally transferred from one person to another
through recognised modes such as sale, gift, lease, mortgage or exchange. Section 6 of the Transfer
of Property Act, 1882 lays down the general rule that property of any kind may be transferred,
subject to statutory restrictions. Transferable property includes immovable property like land and
buildings, movable assets such as vehicles and machinery, intellectual property like patents and
copyrights, and financial instruments such as shares and securities.
Non-transferable property consists of interests that cannot be legally transferred due to their
personal, contingent or restricted nature. Section 6 enumerates specific exceptions to
transferability. Spes succession is, or the mere chance of an heir apparent inheriting property, is
non-transferable under Section 6(a), as affirmed in Official Assignee, Madras v. Sampath Naidu.
Similarly, the right of re-entry, easements apart from the dominant heritage, and interests
restricted to personal enjoyment cannot be transferred. Rights such as future maintenance, a mere
right to sue, public offices, salaries attached to public offices, and pensions are expressly non-
transferable.
Section 6 also prohibits transfers opposed to the nature of the interest, transfers for unlawful
objects or consideration, and transfers to legally disqualified persons. Statutory prohibitions
further restrict transfer of certain tenancy or occupancy rights, as recognised in Shanti Prasad v.
Bachchi Devi. Courts have consistently held that these restrictions preserve the purpose, dignity
and legal character of such interests. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The distinction between transferable and non-transferable property is crucial. Transferable
property offers flexibility, marketability and economic value, while non-transferable property is
protected due to its personal, public, religious or statutory character. Section 6 thus balances
freedom of transfer with legal, moral and public policy considerations, ensuring orderly and lawful
transfer of property rights. [Transferable and Non-Transferable Property; Word Count: 289]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/transferable-and-non-
transferable-property/
passages.LOG-P0176:
VIII. Preparation for their particular craft is the only way for musicians to truly master an
instrument. Natural aptitude is one thing, and certainly it is valuable, but it will not carry
someone very far unless it is combined with disciplined practice and years of dedicated
rehearsal. In fact, several musicians have demonstrated that individuals with exceptional
inborn musical gifts can be far surpassed by those who have painstakingly trained themselves
on a particular instrument. Based on these assertions, it is clear that innate natural aptitude
is never sufficient to carry someone to the pinnacle of the musical world.
passages.LOG-P0177:
XVI. Nestled in a misty valley, the peculiar town of Whispersong thrived on hidden logic. Its
library held no books published after 1950, yet scholars prized its historical accuracy. The
baker's display always showed twelve loaves at dawn, unaffected by morning sales. The clock
tower lacked an hour hand, but appointments were always kept. Children playing "Mirror Tag"
changed the rules if it rained, yet they never argued. And though each front door was a unique
color, the colorblind postman never erred.
passages.LOG-P0178:
XVII. Tune in to the U-19 World Cup, and regional South Asian dialects would be almost as audible as
the English twang. There is a Hindi speaker in 10 of the 16 teams that participate in the
tournament; there is at least one cricketer who understands Punjabi in seven teams; and one who
can speak Gujarati, Telugu and Malayalam in four teams. There are Urdu, Tamil, Sinhala, and
Marathi speakers in teams from outside the Subcontinent. Among the 240 cricketers that have
descended on Namibia and Zimbabwe, 92 are either South Asians or have South Asian ancestors,
constituting 26 per cent of the tournament’s stable of players. The pattern is a reflection of the
shifting sands in world cricket. A game that was once segregated on racial lines in Africa, divided
along social lines in England and Australia, that once saw a prominent British politician, Lord
Tebbit, envisage a “loyalty test” for migrants, has become more inclusive and diverse. Two
youngsters of Pakistani descent are the pillars of the England team; two Indians and two Sri
Lankans are regulars in Australia’s side. New Zealand has four Indians. The USA team fielded an
entire side of second-generation Indians, even as their president, Donald Trump, is on a fierce
visa-revoking spree. Cricket is no longer a colonial sport, it has embraced the post-colonial spirit.
The next stage in the evolution would be akin to the situation in football, where immigrants form
the crux of most European powerhouses, notably England, France, Spain, Belgium and Portugal.
The previously rigid Italy, too, has opened the doors for migrants. Similarly, the identity of cricket
as a colonial leftover has changed, as British society has integrated migrants from its former
colonies. The story of migration is also reshaping the world of sports.
Source: From Under 19 World Cup, a message: Cricket has embraced migrant & post-colonial
spirit, Indian Express
passages.LOG-P0179:
XVII. On the remote Crescent Island, an ancient legend speaks of a treasure buried in the heart
of the island's only mountain. The path to the treasure is guarded by four mysterious guides:
Aris, Bren, Cora, and Dax. Among these guides, some are Knights (who always tell the truth)
and some are Knaves (who always lie). A seeker must deduce who is who from their statements

The four guides made the following declarations to a group of explorers:

Bren: "Aris is a Knave. The treasure is not behind the waterfall."
Cora: "At least one of us is a Knave. Dax is a Knight."
Dax: "Cora is a Knave. The treasure is behind the waterfall."


The explorers know that the actual location of the treasure (whether it is or is not behind the
waterfall) is a fixed, independent fact that does not change based on the statements.

XVII. The summer of 2025 served as a severe wake-up call for India's Himalayan states, exposing the
dark side of unchecked travel. Popular destinations like Manali, Mussoorie, and Shimla faced a
crisis known as "overtourism," where the sheer volume of visitors far exceeded what the local
environment and infrastructure could support. Reports from Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh
described a chaotic scene: tourists were stuck in gridlocked traffic for hours on fragile mountain
roads, while local residents faced acute shortages of water and electricity. The surge in visitors has
pushed these "carrying capacities"—the maximum population a region can sustain without
collapsing—to their breaking point.
This crisis is not merely an inconvenience for holidaymakers; it is an environmental disaster in
the making. To cater to the rush, there has been a frenzy of unregulated construction, with hotels
and guesthouses springing up on unstable slopes. This haphazard development blocks natural
drainage paths, significantly increasing the risk of landslides and flash floods during the monsoon.
Critics argue that state governments have historically prioritized revenue over regulation,
focusing on collecting tourism taxes while ignoring the mounting waste management crisis. The
mountains are now littered with plastic and debris that local municipalities simply cannot process.
In response, experts are calling for a radical shift in how we manage hill tourism. New policy
suggestions include implementing a "green tax" or an entry permit system to limit vehicle

numbers in sensitive zones. There is also a push to promote "off-beat" rural tourism to disperse
crowds away from congested hubs. However, unless strict limits are enforced, India risks
destroying the very serenity and natural beauty that draw millions to the Himalayas in the first
place.
Source: Analysis based on The Geostrata and National Herald reports on Himalayan overtourism
(2025)
passages.LOG-P0183: A rapidly growing food delivery company, QuickBasket, had recently expanded its services to several smaller cities. Although customer orders increased significantly, the company soon began facing complaints regarding delayed deliveries, incorrect orders, and poor customer support. Employees working in different city offices also reported confusion about delivery procedures and inconsistent instructions from managers. Concerned that these issues could damage the company's reputation, the board appointed an operations consultant to study the organization and recommend solutions. The consultant interacted with senior managers, delivery executives, customer support staff, restaurant partners, and customers to understand the problems more clearly. After reviewing delivery records, customer complaints, and employee feedback, the consultant found that different regional offices were following separate systems for assigning orders and tracking deliveries. Many delivery executives had also not received proper training in handling customer complaints or using the company's updated mobile application efficiently. To improve operations, the consultant suggested introducing a unified digital tracking system across all branches, conducting training workshops for employees, and creating a centralized customer support department to respond to complaints more quickly. However, some regional managers opposed the reforms because they believed that a common system would reduce their control over local operations. To address these concerns, the consultant organized meetings with managers, explained the long-term benefits of coordination, and encouraged employees to provide suggestions before changes were implemented. The overall objective was to create a more efficient, customer-friendly, and coordinated organization capable of maintaining growth in a competitive market.

XVIII. In a major move to combat lifestyle diseases, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
(FSSAI) has introduced tougher rules for food labeling in 2025, fundamentally changing how
packaged food is sold. The most significant update is the mandatory "Front-of-Pack Labeling"
(FOPL) for items classified as High in Fat, Salt, and Sugar (HFSS). Previously, nutritional
information was buried in tiny, unreadable text on the back of the packet. The new norms require
this critical data to be displayed boldly on the front, acting as an immediate warning to
consumers. This shift is designed to help buyers make healthier choices instantly, without needing
a degree in nutrition to understand the ingredients list. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The regulations also target the misleading "health halo" that many brands use to sell processed
foods. For instance, if a company claims its cookies are "rich in protein" or "zero cholesterol," they
must now provide laboratory-verified proof to back up these assertions. The FSSAI has set a strict
timeline, with a compliance deadline of July 1, 2025, for companies to update their packaging.
This has caused some friction in the industry, with manufacturers arguing that changing labels is
expensive and that the new warning symbols might "demonize" traditional Indian snacks.
However, health experts argue that these strict measures are necessary because India is rapidly
becoming the "diabetes capital" of the world. By forcing transparency, the government aims to
shift the responsibility back to the manufacturers. Furthermore, even restaurant chains and
online food delivery apps are now required to display calorie counts for their dishes, ensuring that
consumers are aware of what they are eating, whether they are cooking at home or ordering in.
Source: Expanded analysis based on FSSAI’s 2025 Nutrition Labelling Amendment coverage by
Envirocare Labs.
passages.LOG-P0186:
XVI. India's expansion of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPJ), particularly through platforms like
UPI and Bhashini, has been hailed as a global model for financial inclusion and linguistic
accessibility. However, as the state pivots toward "Data-Led Governance," a critical ethical
divide has emerged. The premise of DPI is that by digitizing citizen data, the government can
deliver services with unprecedented precision, cutting through the red tape of traditional
bureaucracy.
The friction point lies in the concept of "informed consent." In a country with varying levels of
digital literacy, the act of clicking "I Agree" on a government portal often lacks substantive
understanding. Furthermore, the aggregation of health, financial, and biometric data under a
single digital identity creates a "honey pot" for cyber-attacks and potential state surveillance.
Proponents argue that the collective benefit of efficient welfare delivery outweighs individual
privacy concerns in a developing economy. Yet, this utilitarian calculus ignores the fact that

privacy is not a luxury for the elite but a safeguard for the marginalized against
administrative overreach. As we integrate AI into this infrastructure to predict citizen needs,
the risk of "algorithmic bias"—where historical prejudices are coded into service delivery—
becomes a tangible threat to equity.
Source: htips:/ /www.publicationsdivision.nic.in/journals/Journalarchives/Yojana/ Yojana-
English/2024/February/
passages.LOG-P0187:
XVI. In criminal jurisprudence, the doctrine of mens rea bifurcates into intention and knowledge,
constituting the foundational mental elements requisite for establishing culpability in most penal
offences. Intention denotes the deliberate purpose or conscious design accompanying the
commission of an act, whereas knowledge signifies cognitive awareness of the probable
consequences emanating from such conduct, notwithstanding the absence of desire for the specific
result. Indian criminal law recognizes a hierarchical gradation of mental states, and this
taxonomy materially influences both the characterization of the offence and the quantum of
liability imposed. The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) distinctly demarcates acts perpetrated
intentionally, knowingly, or with rashness. Culpable homicide as contemplated under Section 299
IPC may be predicated upon either the intention to cause death or knowledge that the act is
imminently likely to cause death, whereas death occasioned by rash or negligent conduct falls
within the ambit of Section 304A IPC. Certain factual matrices, however, obfuscate this doctrinal
distinction. When an act is executed with knowledge that harm may potentially ensue, yet
accompanied by subjective optimism that adverse consequences might be averted, penal liability
may nevertheless crystallize. This principle assumes particular salience where the accused
consciously undertook a calculated risk and the deleterious consequence remained objectively
foreseeable. This interpretive framework ensures that criminal liability is not imposed
capriciously or arbitrarily, affirming that the subjective mental state of the accused remains the
analytical fulcrum in determining guilt except where the legislature has expressly displaced this
requirement through statutory fiat in specified enactments such as those governing statutory rape
or public health violations, wherein strict liability principles supersede the traditional mens rea
requirement.
passages.LOG-P0188: In the years before Lehman Brothers went bust in 2008, plunging the world into financial crisis, macroeconomists were understandably worried. But they worried about the wrong thing: not over-indebted American banks, but over-thrifty Asian economies. According to this theory, Asia's determination to accumulate dollar reserves was depressing interest rates, tempting Americans to overspend. The upshot was that Asia earned more than it spent, resulting in large trade surpluses. This enabled America to spend more than it earned, reflected in a yawning current-account deficit. These "global imbalances" are back. The new imbalances are not quite as big as those of two decades ago. The world's deficit countries had a combined current-account gap of 1.6% of global GDP in 2025, compared with a peak of 2.6% in 2006. President Donald Trump cited America's deficit to justify his "Liberation Day" tariffs last year. President Emmanuel Macron of France called China's surpluses "unbearable" on his visit to Beijing in December. One answer is America's budget deficit. Tax cuts or higher welfare spending increase American consumption and reduce saving. That can lift interest rates and thus the dollar-which makes exports less competitive, deepening the trade deficit. Other commentators are equally confident that the culprit is once again Asia, especially China. China subsidises its manufacturers, resulting in excess capacity. What these firms cannot sell at home, they dump abroad. This crowds out local manufacturers, destroying jobs and obliging countries like America to increase their fiscal deficits to restore demand and curb unemployment. What has suppressed domestic spending in China is a property slump. If China is the culprit for imbalances, it has perpetrated more a blunder than a crime. Its big fiscal deficits are a political choice not an economic necessity. The causes of global imbalances are not, then, as clear as some commentators allege. All of the suspects are implicated. But the ending could still be bad.

XVIII. Facial Recognition and Digital Privacy Concerns: As artificial intelligence advances, facial
recognition technology has become increasingly powerful and accessible. Governments and private
companies can now identify individuals in crowds, track movement patterns, and monitor
behaviour with minimal human oversight. This creates unprecedented privacy risks. Consider
what happens when facial recognition is used without consent at airports, shopping malls, or
public protests: individuals lose the ability to move through public spaces anonymously. In
authoritarian regimes, this technology enables mass surveillance systems that suppress dissent
and control populations. Even in democracies, the absence of clear consent mechanisms means
people cannot opt out of being scanned and tracked.
The core problem is that current regulations lag far behind the technology's capabilities. Data
protection laws often require consent before collecting personal information, but facial recognition
systems operate silently and invisibly. A person walking down the street has no way to know if
their face has been captured, analyzed, and stored in a database. This asymmetry of power—
where authorities can watch citizens but citizens cannot know they are being watched—
undermines the basic principles of democratic society. Facial recognition technology also amplifies
bias: studies show that these systems are significantly less accurate for people with darker skin
tones, creating disparities in both surveillance and error rates.
Addressing this crisis requires explicit legal protections: banning facial recognition in sensitive
contexts like protests and public spaces, requiring transparent reporting of surveillance activities,
and building independent oversight mechanisms to review government access to biometric data.
Without strong regulatory action, facial recognition will become a tool for unchecked state and
corporate power, fundamentally changing the relationship between individuals and institutions.
Source: Online, December 2025 & OHCHR Joint Declaration on AI
passages.LOG-P0191:
XV.	The Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, popularly known as the Anti-Defection Law, was
introduced to combat the evil of political defections motivated by the lure of office or material
advantage. However, recent political crises across various states have exposed glaring loopholes in
its architecture. The law designates the Speaker of the legislative assembly as the sole adjudicator
of defection petitions. This creates an inherent conflict of interest, as the Speaker is almost always
a member of the ruling party and depends on their goodwill for continuance in office. Consequently,
adjudication is often marred by partisan bias. Petitions against opposition members are decided
with remarkable haste, whereas those against ruling party legislators are kept pending
indefinitely, effectively defeating the law's purpose.
Furthermore, the 'merger' exception under paragraph 4 of the Schedule allows a two-thirds
majority of a legislature party to merge with another party without facing disqualification.
Originally intended to protect genuine ideological realignments, this provision is now frequently
weaponized to engineer wholesale defections. Critics argue that this legitimizes retail defection
while merely raising the threshold to wholesale defection. To restore constitutional morality, legal
experts advocate stripping the Speaker of this adjudicatory power. Instead, an independent
tribunal headed by retired judges or the Election Commission should decide disqualification
matters. While the Supreme Court has repeatedly urged Parliament to amend the Constitution to
effect this change, legislative inertia persists. Until the institutional mechanism is overhauled, the
Tenth Schedule will remain a tool for political maneuvering rather than a shield against it.
Source: Edited and Excerpted from:
https://prsindia.org/files/parliament/discussion_papers/The_Anti-Defection_Law.pdf

XVII. When spring rolls around in the northern hemisphere, so do conversations about “No Mow
May.” Homeowners forgo mowing, allowing otherwise hidden flowers to bloom in your lawn,
increasing your yard’s biodiversity and providing food for pollinator concerns like these, No
Mow May ors like bees. However, scientists have increasingly questioned whether this trend,
which began in the United Kingdom, is compatible with United States lawns. Many U.S.
lawns are filled with non-native species like dandelions (Taraxacum officinale), which
Europeans colonists introduced to North America. These plants are not necessarily a good food
source for native pollinators as they lack certain important amino acids that make nectar and
pollen nutritious. Because of concerns like these, No Mow May has actually “become quite
controversial” in the U.S. I mean, who knew dandelions could be so controversial?
“No Mow May” started in 2018 as a campaign by the U.K. organization Plantlife. The group
originally coined the slogan to encourage local U.K. councils to manage green spaces more like
traditional hay meadows to increase biodiversity. Historically, workers who tended hay
meadows let them grow long throughout spring and most of the summer, only cutting them at
the end of summer to make hay. Plantlife picked May as the month to focus on for two main
reasons: May is the month that many U.K. grassland species start to flower (although climate
change is shifting that), and May is also when farmers traditionally removed animals from
hay meadows so they could grow. Plantlife suggested local authorities test out the hay meadow
management style with “No Mow May.”
Plantlife soon realized that the slogan was catching on with the public, and that “this could be
a really great way to engage the public about the importance of grasslands. In the U.K.,
“people’s lawns are often kind of relic grasslands,” and letting them grow can reveal native
flowers they didn’t know they had in their lawn. These flowers provide nectar and pollen for
native bees and other local pollinators that evolved alongside these plants. Plantlife chose May
for its campaign because it aligns with traditional hay meadow management, not because
there was specific scientific evidence about not mowing in May. Since the campaign started,
there has been at least one study examining its effects: In 2022, Ecological Solutions and
Evidence published a paper showing that un-mowed grassland plots in the U.K. produced
more nectar in mid-late May than mowed plots, providing more food for native pollinators. But
in the United States, the effects of No Mow May aren’t necessarily the same. /Environment;
Word Count: 423]

XVI. India's Urban Mobility Crisis: India stands at a critical crossroads. Its urban centers are
growing rapidly with more people buying private vehicles, creating severe traffic congestion, air
pollution, and a declining quality of life. This crisis did not happen by accident—it is the direct
result of decades of planning that prioritized cars over public transportation. Most Indian cities
have focused heavily on building metro rail systems while neglecting buses and other transport
modes. This "one size fits all" approach has created serious problems: areas without metro
coverage have almost no transit options, forcing people to buy cars and motorcycles.
The real issue is that governments have been moving cars, not people. A city like Bengaluru has
more buses per mile than most cities, yet it performs poorly compared to international standards
because it lacks good last-mile connectivity and pedestrian-friendly streets. Projects like tunnel
roads and coastal highways seem smart temporarily because they reduce traffic, but they
ultimately invite more vehicles onto the roads—a phenomenon called "induced demand."
Meanwhile, cities are destroying valuable public spaces for these projects without solving the
actual problem. www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, there are positive signs. Survey data shows that most people are willing to use quality
public transportation if available. Metro systems are expanding rapidly, and some cities are
redesigning streets with wide pedestrian paths. Bengaluru plans to deploy 10,000 buses in coming
years. For real progress, citizens must demand better urban planning from their governments and
choose public transit over personal vehicles. Only a fundamental mindset shift from "moving cars"
to "moving people" can create the liveable cities India needs.
Source: The Journal Club (Bit News), September 2025; India's Urban Mobility Crisis

XVII. In early 2026, a landmark case reached the Supreme Court where a group of youth activists
sued the government for what they described as “intergenerational climate injustice.” The
petitioners argued that the state’s continued reliance on coal-fired power plants, despite the
existence of viable green alternatives, violates the fundamental right to a clean environment
for future generations. According to the petitioners, the environmental harm caused by
present-day policy choices will be borne primarily by citizens of tomorrow, who have no
representation in current decision-making processes. This controversy brings to the fore the
legal doctrine of the “Public Trust,” which posits that the state is not the owner of natural
resources but merely a trustee holding them for the benefit of the public, including those yet to
be born.
Opponents of such climate litigation, however, strongly contest this approach. They argue that
courts are ill-equipped to handle “polycentric” issues, namely problems that involve complex
and interconnected economic, social, and technical trade-offs. In their view, decisions relating
to energy policy should remain the exclusive domain of the legislature and executive, as these
institutions are democratically accountable and better positioned to assess competing public
interests. They warn that a judicial mandate directing the shutdown of coal-fired power plants
could result in immediate energy shortages, thereby affecting millions of current citizens who
rely on affordable power for their livelihoods and daily needs.
At this juncture, the “precautionary principle”’—which supports taking preventive measures to
avoid future harm even when scientific certainty is incomplete—comes into direct conflict with
the “necessity of development.” The court must now determine whether the “Constitution of
today” can adequately protect the “citizens of tomorrow” without the judiciary overstepping its
institutional boundaries or encroaching upon the functions of the other branches of
government.

XVIII. If there are two things the internet loves talking about, its conspiracy theories, and who may or may
not be a narcissist. Misinformation and conspiratorial thinking are long-running concerns, while
narcissism has become TikTok’s favourite armchair diagnosis. Research shows the two concepts,
though seemingly separate, may actually be closely linked. In my new research published in the
Journal of Personality and Individual Differences, more than 600 people completed surveys, and the
findings show higher scores on measures of narcissism were linked to belief in conspiracy theories and
misinformation. Importantly, this result held true regardless of how educated the participants were.
Scholarly evidence shows people with lower levels of education are more likely to believe in conspiracy
theories. But that’s only part of the story. We also know that historically, conspiracy theories have done
well in times of uncertainty, including during war, economic downturn and widespread hardship (such
as the COVID pandemic). www.lawpreptutorial.com
A prominent explanation for this is that conspiracy beliefs serve underlying psychological needs. These
include providing answers when things are unclear or uncertain, providing a sense of control by
identifying a powerful group to take action against, and for social reasons, such as showing others
which political groups you belong to and signalling loyalty to those groups. I wanted to find out when
educated people might also “fall down the rabbit hole”, and learn more about which psychological needs
lead them to do so. The participants had varying levels of education, ranging from high school or less
through to having a masters or doctorate. They also had a variety of political beliefs. People who scored
higher in narcissistic traits were more accepting of conspiracy theories and misinformation.
Importantly, this was true regardless of how educated the person was. The results showed these traits
might offset the differences linked to education. When these traits were above average, highly educated
people were just as likely to endorse these beliefs as those without any formal education.
Education often provides people with skills in evaluating evidence, critical thinking and a shared
understanding of how we can find truth. However, humans are quite good at “motivated reasoning”:
using reasoning skills to come to pleasing conclusions because we want to believe something. This type
of reasoning is often linked to unfounded beliefs — those without evidence. When people feel superior to
experts, want to feel special, or need a concrete answer during uncertain times, they might use their
reasoning to hold certain beliefs despite a lack of evidence. My research suggests educated people are
not immune to this.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://theconversation.com/why-do-educated-people-
fall-for-conspiracy-theories-it-could-be-narcissism-270169

Agreement with India will boost exports and open new opportunities for farmers, growers and
businesses, describing the pact as a landmark deal with one of the world’s fastest-growing major
economies. India and New Zealand have concluded negotiations on the FTA, which is expected to take
effect in seven to eight months. The agreement aims to enhance market access and promote
investment flows between the two countries, including a foreign direct investment commitment of $20
billion over a period of 15 years. "We've concluded a Free Trade Agreement with India. This will open

with Oman in December. The agreement with Oman will give India more temporary employment visas

"intensive" and said his government has worked extremely hard to prioritise and invest in the

agreement were initiated during Luxon’s visit to India in March 2025, when the two leaders agreed on

SECTION IV
XV. ‘In an era where urban safety is paramount, governments worldwide are increasingly deploying
Al-powered surveillance systems in public spaces. Proponents argue that these technologies,
equipped with facial recognition and behavioural analysis, significantly reduce crime rates by
enabling real-time threat detection. For instance, cities like London and Singapore report a 20-
30% drop in petty crimes since implementation. The reasoning is straightforward: deterrence
through omnipresence. When potential offenders know they are being watched by an unblinking
digital eye, rational choice theory suggests they will opt for compliance over transgression.
Moreover, these systems allow law enforcement to allocate resources efficiently, focusing human
officers on high-risk interventions rather than routine patrols.
Critics, however, contend that such surveillance erodes fundamental privacy rights, creating a
panopticon society where citizens self-censor out of fear. Ethical concerns intensify with
documented cases of algorithmic bias—studies show facial recognition tools misidentify people of
colour at rates up to 35% higher than others, leading to wrongful detentions. This not only
undermines trust in institutions but also perpetuates systemic inequalities. Governments counter
that anonymization protocols and human oversight mitigate these risks, yet evidence from
independent audits reveals persistent flaws. The core tension lies in balancing collective security
against individual liberty: is the marginal crime reduction worth the slippery slope toward
totalitarianism? Policymakers must assume that technological perfection is unattainable; thus,
robust regulatory frameworks—such as mandatory transparency reports and independent
audits—are essential. Without them, public backlash could stall innovation. Ultimately, the
argument hinges on societal values: a polity prioritizing safety may embrace surveillance, while
one valuing autonomy might reject it. As AI evolves, the debate demands nuanced reasoning, not
binary absolutes, to forge policies that neither stifle progress nor sacrifice principles.
Source: Extracted from: The Ethics of AI Surveillance in Public Spaces
passages.LOG-P0202:
SECTION IV
XVII. At Dubai’s Madinat Jumeirah, visitors moved quietly between installations, pausing to
photograph sculptural works, leaning in to decipher mirrored text, and standing longer than
usual inside sound-filled rooms that invited reflection. Beyond the fairgrounds, however, the
mood across the region was markedly different. In the weeks leading up to Art Dubai’s 20th
edition, headlines were dominated by the escalating conflict between Iran and Israel, travel
disruptions and renewed uncertainty across the Gulf. That contrast, between a region
confronting war and an art fair built around dialogue, memory and exchange, shaped much of
this year’s edition.
After weeks of uncertainty, including a calendar shift from its original April dates to May 15-
17 amid regional tensions, Art Dubai opened with a quieter energy. There was less emphasis
on spectacle, more space for conversation, and a sense that both audiences and organisers
were approaching the anniversary edition with different priorities. As Art Dubai marks its
20th year, the fair appears less interested in market theatre than in a more urgent question:
what role can culture play when the world outside feels increasingly unstable?
What began in 2007 as the Gulf Art Fair has, over two decades, evolved far beyond its
commercial origins. Today, Art Dubai stands as one of West Asia’s most influential cultural
institutions, mirroring both Dubai’s own transformation and the emergence of the region as a
serious force in the global art conversation. Its journey has been shaped by defining moments.
In its early years, the fair helped position the Gulf on the global cultural map, contributing to
a broader regional shift towards soft power, creative economies and post-oil cultural identity.
It has also navigated moments of controversy. In 2012, reports surrounding the removal of a
politically sensitive work by Iranian artist Khosrow Hassanzadeh sparked debate around
censorship, political expression and the boundaries artists negotiate in the region. The fair has
always been about more than commerce. In times of crisis, culture becomes something people
turn to for renewal, healing and connection.
Unlike many established art fairs that remain anchored to western markets, Art Dubai has
consistently positioned itself as a meeting point for artists, collectors and curators from
geographies often underrepresented in the global art market. Notably, while Indian galleries
were absent from this year’s edition, Indian artistic voices remained strongly present. Nearly a
dozen artists from India featured across the fair, underscoring the country’s enduring creative

XVI. Search, Seizure, and Attachment: CrPC and BNSS Compared
The investigation of a criminal offence involves three critical pre-trial powers: search, seizure,
and attachment. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), Sections 93-103 govern
search procedures. A Magistrate may issue a search warrant where evidence is not otherwise
obtainable or where items are suspected to be stolen or used in a crime. Section 165 CrPC
permits a police officer to search without a warrant during investigation if delay would
prejudice the case. All searches must be conducted in the presence of independent witnesses
called panchas, and compliance with Section 100 CrPC requires at least two respectable
inhabitants of the locality, preparation of a panchnama, and provision of a copy of the seized
articles list to the occupant.
Regarding seizure, Section 102 CrPC empowers police to seize property suspected to be stolen
or connected to a crime, with a mandatory report to the Magistrate. Sections 451-452 CrPC
confer judicial authority to dispose of or return property during and after trial. Attachment
under Section 83 CrPC applies to property of proclaimed offenders declared under Section 82,
covering both movable and immovable property. Section 105 CrPC extends attachment to
properties linked to offences committed outside India.www.lptedtech.com
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, replaces CrPC with significant
modernisation. BNSS contains search-warrant/search-related provisions in Sections 96-105
and separately provides for search by police officer during investigation under Section 185,
introducing electronic records and gender-sensitive procedures for searches involving women.
Section 106 BNSS corresponds broadly to police power to seize certain property. Section 105
BNSS introduces audio-video recording of search and seizure. Section 107 BNSS deals with
attachment, forfeiture, or restoration of property derived from criminal activity. Sections 87—
88 BNSS address attachment of proclaimed offenders' property, enabling digital notice
issuance and faster recovery proceedings.
[Word Count: 268]
Source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 —
Chapters VII, IX, XII

passages.LOG-P0205:
XV. In public law and regulatory governance, delegated legislation plays a crucial role in
implementing statutory objectives while balancing administrative efficiency and
democratic accountability. Legislatures often enact broad framework statutes and delegate
rule-making powers to the executive or specialised authorities to fill in operational details.
Such delegation is considered necessary in modern governance, given the technical
complexity and evolving nature of regulation. However, this delegation is not unlimited. A
fundamental constitutional principle governing delegated legislation is that essential
legislative functions cannot be delegated. The legislature must lay down the policy,
purpose, and guiding principles of the law. Delegated authorities may only determine
details, procedures, or technical standards within this framework. If the parent statute
confers unfettered discretion without clear guidance, the delegation may be struck down
as excessive or unconstitutional. Judicial review of delegated legislation primarily focuses
on ultra vires control. A rule or regulation may be invalidated if it exceeds the scope of
authority granted by the parent statute, contradicts the statute’s objectives, or violates
constitutional provisions. Courts also examine whether delegated legislation is arbitrary,
unreasonable, or manifestly unjust, especially when it affects fundamental rights or
imposes penalties. At the same time, courts recognise that delegated legislation enjoys a
presumption of validity. Judicial intervention is cautious, particularly in areas involving
technical expertise, economic regulation, or public welfare. The role of the court is not to
assess the wisdom of the rule but to ensure that it remains within legal boundaries. Thus,


delegated legislation reflects a delicate balance: it enables flexible and responsive
governance, yet remains constrained by constitutional limits, legislative intent, and the
principles of accountability and rule of law.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.lawctopus.com/clatalogue/clat-
ug/delegated-legislation-in-administrative-law/, 24-09-2024
passages.LOG-P0206:
XVII. India’s cloud is not only virtual — it is increasingly physical, resource-intensive and expanding
at an extraordinary pace. As digital adoption deepens, artificial intelligence scales, and
businesses shift relentlessly to cloud-based operations, the country is experiencing a wave of
hyperscale and colocation data-centre construction unlike anything seen before. These
facilities have quietly become the invisible scaffolding of India’s digital economy, powering
everything from payments and logistics to e-governance, entertainment, healthcare, and an
emerging AI industry. They bring investment, jobs, efficiency, and the promise of a
technologically-advanced future.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Yet, beneath this progress lies an uncomfortable truth: data centres are energy-hungry and
water-thirsty, and their rapid growth risks creating a severe environmental and hydrological
burden that India is not prepared to handle. The scale of expansion explains the growing
alarm. India’s data-centre capacity has surged in recent years, and analysts forecast that it
may multiply several-fold by the end of this decade as AI computing, 5G applications and
cloud services proliferate. Each additional megawatt of computing load generates enormous
heat that must be dissipated constantly, every hour of every day.
To manage this heat, most large centres rely heavily on water-intensive cooling techniques
such as evaporative cooling towers. Independent studies estimate that if this expansion
continues unchecked, India’s data-centre sector could collectively withdraw hundreds of
billions of litres of water annually within a few years. These numbers are not abstractions.

Data centres are concentrated in coastal and metropolitan hubs like Mumbai, Chennai,
Hyderabad, Bengaluru and the National Capital Region — precisely those regions that
already face severe water scarcity during peak summers, chronic groundwater depletion, and
frequent competition between residential demand, agriculture, and industrial use. The
creation of sprawling digital infrastructures that depend on constant water supply in water-
stressed basins poses a clear and imminent risk.
The question then arises: why do data centres require so much water in the first place? The
answer lies in basic physics and economics. High-density servers, especially those supporting
GPU-heavy AI workloads, generate intense heat. Water-cooled evaporative towers remain the
industry's preferred solution because they are efficient and cost-effective at scale. A single
hyperscale data centre can require millions of litres of water per day at peak operational loads.
Beyond direct consumption, the indirect water footprint is equally significant: electricity
generation from thermal power plants, manufacturing of servers and components,
construction of massive concrete-and-steel facilities, and water treatment processes all
contribute to the sector’s overall hydrological impact. [Word Count: 400]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https: / /timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/voices /data-centres-an-emerging-environmental-
menace/
passages.LOG-P0207:
XVII. The recent nationwide strike by a vast cohort of gig workers has exposed the precariousness
embedded within India’s emerging labour framework for platform-mediated work. This unrest
unfolded immediately after the Labour Ministry released draft Rules to operationalise the revised
labour codes, highlighting a fundamental disjunction between regulatory intent and lived labour
realities. While these Rules formally acknowledge gig workers within the social security
architecture, they conspicuously exclude them from statutory protections relating to wages and
working conditions. By severing gig work from the traditional employment relationship for wage
determination, the framework relegates platforms to the limited obligation of making aggregate
contributions to a social security fund, leaving core worker grievances unresolved. The Code on
Wages, though ostensibly universal, exempts gig workers by categorising their labour as distinct
from employment, thereby permitting algorithmic rate reductions and opaque incentive
mechanisms to persist unchecked. Similarly, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working
Conditions Rules adopt a compliance-centric model predicated on employer reporting via the
Shram Suvidha Portal — an approach ill-suited to the dispersed, app-mediated nature of gig
labour. In effect, social security emerges as the sole substantive reform, yet even here, access
remains contingent and procedurally burdensome. Under the draft provisions, gig workers must
register on a designated portal, while aggregators are required to periodically upload engagement
data. Eligibility hinges on minimum thresholds of 90 days with a single platform or 120
cumulative days across platforms within a financial year. Although multiple engagements within
a single day may be counted multiplicatively, this technical accommodation fails to constrain
platform control over work allocation. More critically, such temporal thresholds risk penalising
workers engaged in unpaid care labour, suffering illness, maternity-related interruptions, or
facing demand volatility beyond their control.

Consequently, the draft Rules necessitate substantive redesign to ensure that social security is not
merely nominal but operationally meaningful. Threshold criteria must incorporate explicit
safeguards against involuntary work discontinuities and prevent lapses arising from transient
downturns. Furthermore, the framework must delineate the specific benefits available, prescribe
minimum entitlements supported by the Social Security Fund, and establish a transparent, time-
bound mechanism for claims, grievances, and appeals independent of platform discretion. Finally,
procedural transparency must be institutionalised. Aggregators should be mandated to furnish
workers with regular statements detailing tasks completed, hours logged, earnings accrued, and
deductions imposed, alongside a robust mechanism for contesting inaccuracies. Absent such
reforms, the proposed regime risks entrenching the very structural insecurity that precipitated
collective action among gig workers, rendering regulatory recognition hollow rather than
transformative.

PASSAGE 18
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) now expects the Indian economy to grow by 6.8% in 2025-
26. This is higher than RBI’s 6.5% projection made in August. It has also revised its inflation
forecast for the current fiscal year downward from 3.1% in August to 2.6% now. This is the
lowest-ever inflation rate, within the RBI's 2%-6% target band, since the current series began
in 2012-13. And a 6.8% growth rate is above India’s potential growth rate. These numbers
paint a perfect picture for the macro economy that is doing good in terms of growth without
triggering inflation. Is the Indian economy in the so-called Goldilocks state, where it is neither
too hot nor too cold? There is good reason to exercise some caution in jumping to this
conclusion.

The RBI has raised its economic growth forecast to 6.8% for 2025-26, up from 6.5%, and
lowered its inflation forecast to 2.6%. However, this improved outlook may be due to lower-


than-expected inflation, not stronger economic momentum. As a result, the nominal growth
rate may fall below the budget's 10.1% target, potentially limiting government fiscal space.
Given these uncertainties, the MPC's decision to keep interest rates unchanged is considered
appropriate, as it waits to assess both positive and negative economic factors before making
further changes. The Indian economy isn’t in as sweet a spot as the latest growth and inflation
projections suggest it is — but there is nothing that suggests a deep-rooted crisis as well, and
this is exactly why the MPC’s pause is a prudent one.

SOURCE:https://www.hindustantimes.com/editorials/dose-of-caution-in-the-optimism-
101759332650649.html
passages.LOG-P0211:
XVIII. The live concerts industry is rapidly becoming a significant focus for major financial investors,
signalling its emergence as a distinct and valuable business asset. This article explores the
key reasons behind this transformation, examining how concerts generate revenue, why big
money is getting involved, and their substantial economic impact. Once seen purely as
entertainment, live concerts are now emerging as a serious investment category. Institutional
investors, private equity firms, and tech platforms are taking note - driven by the sector’s
resilient demand, diverse revenue streams, and cultural staying power. This article explores
the forces behind this transformation and why live events may soon be viewed alongside
traditional asset classes.

Live concerts offer a distinct investment proposition. They operate with minimal correlation to
public markets and are largely shielded from stock market volatility, making them an
attractive option for portfolio diversification. The industry is protected by high barriers to
entry - limited premier venues, entrenched promoter relationships, and complex logistics -
which makes established players especially valuable.
A major factor fuelling investor interest is the monetization of intellectual property.
Innovations like Live Capture (concert livestreaming) and immersive experiences such as
Location-Based Entertainment are unlocking scalable, repeatable revenue models. Globally,
IP monetization in the live events space is expected to grow from $3 billion currently to $23
billion over the next decade. The investor approach is also evolving. Rather than backing
individual events, many are building portfolios of live experiences to distribute risk while
improving long-term returns. As a cornerstone of the growing “experience economy”, live
concerts have shown remarkable resilience during economic downturns, reflecting a shift in
consumer priorities from material goods to memorable experiences.
Live concerts have outgrown their reliance on ticket sales. They now generate income through
a wide range of channels, each with strong monetization potential. Dynamic pricing has
transformed how tickets are sold. Much like airlines or hotels, ticket prices adjust in real time
based on demand, maximizing revenue while rewarding early buyers. However, this model
requires transparency and ethical implementation, as unfair or overly opportunistic pricing
can quickly erode fan trust. The secondary ticketing market is also booming. Globally, it is
projected to reach $73.4 billion by 2033. Event organizers often keep original ticket prices
relatively low to maintain accessibility, brand equity, and audience loyalty, leaving the resale
market to capture the true market value. In India, this trend is just beginning to formalize. A
key milestone was Zomato’s resale feature for its 2024 “Feeding India” concert, signalling the
start of structured secondary ticketing in the country. [Word Count: 421]
